common_name: Heritage River Birch (Classic Cream-Salmon Exfoliating-Bark Selection)

planting.note: Plant container-grown trees in fall or early spring before new growth starts; Heritage is the classic, original patented river birch cultivar, selected for exceptionally showy exfoliating cream-to-salmon bark.

directions: Plant in full sun to partial shade in moist, slightly acidic, well-drained to periodically flooded soil. Heritage was the original, patented selection of native river birch that launched the cultivar's popularity in the nursery trade, chosen for its exceptionally showy, exfoliating bark that peels in large, papery sheets of cream, salmon-pink, and cinnamon-brown, a striking year-round ornamental feature most dramatic on multi-trunk specimens. It tolerates the heat, humidity, and periodic flooding of Gulf South conditions far better than most birches, which require cooler summers, making it valuable along streams, ponds, and in rain gardens. Fall color is a modest yellow, and the tree grows relatively fast, 2 to 3 feet per year when young, providing dappled shade suitable for understory plantings.
sources: North Carolina State Extension — Betula nigra Cultivars
University of Florida IFAS Extension — Birch Trees for Florida

common_name: Little King River Birch (Fox Valley Dwarf Compact Selection)

planting.note: Plant container-grown trees or shrubs in fall or early spring before new growth starts; Little King, sold under the trade name Fox Valley, is a true dwarf river birch reaching only 10-12 feet, fitting spaces too small for standard river birch.

directions: Plant in full sun to partial shade in moist, slightly acidic, well-drained to periodically flooded soil. Little King, marketed under the trade name Fox Valley, is a genuine dwarf selection of river birch that stays a compact, dense, multi-stemmed shrub or small tree only 10 to 12 feet tall, retaining the same attractive exfoliating cream-to-tan bark and fine-textured foliage as full-sized river birch cultivars but scaled for foundation plantings, small yards, or as a large shrub border specimen. It tolerates the heat, humidity, and periodic flooding of Gulf South conditions well. Fall color is a modest yellow, and it needs minimal pruning to maintain its naturally rounded, dense form.
sources: North Carolina State Extension — Betula nigra Cultivars

planting.note: Plant nursery stock in spring or early fall in well-drained, average soil in full sun to partial shade; Traveller is a weeping Texas redbud selection with glossy, thick, drought-tolerant foliage and cascading branches, discovered in Oklahoma.

directions: Plant in well-drained, average soil in full sun to partial shade; the Texas redbud parentage gives Traveller notably better drought tolerance than straight Cercis canadensis. Traveller is a strongly weeping, cascading redbud discovered in Oklahoma, its arching, drooping branches forming a distinctive umbrella-like canopy that requires staking to establish trunk height before the weeping habit takes over. It bears the classic rosy-pink, pea-like spring flowers on bare branches before the glossy, thick, heat- and drought-tolerant leaves typical of Texas redbud emerge, followed by good yellow fall color. Water deeply during the first two years to establish the root system, then supplement only during dry spells once established.
